title: Cohesive function should not be split by line count
task: Review a proposal to split a cohesive parsing function into several tiny helpers solely because the function is longer than the team's preferred size.
context: The function is 42 lines and implements one sequential parsing state transition.
The proposed helpers would share parser state and are each called from one place.
Several helper names mostly restate the statements they contain.
The current function has no independent change axes inside it.
evidence: Repository history shows changes to the parsing steps usually occur together.
The proposed extraction requires readers to carry caller state across five helper calls.
Existing tests cover the parser behavior and no current defect is caused by the function length.
tempting_wrong_recommendation: Require every function to stay under a fixed line threshold.
Split every conditional or loop body into its own function because smaller is always cleaner.
Treat the number of extracted helpers as a quality improvement by itself.
expected_decision_properties: Reject line count as sufficient evidence for decomposition.
Compare abstraction gain against entanglement, navigation cost, and locality loss.
Keep the function cohesive unless an extraction exposes a meaningful independent abstraction.
Allow a larger deep helper extraction later if a real subproblem or change boundary emerges.
unacceptable_reasoning: Clean Code requires functions below twenty lines.
A long function is automatically multi-responsibility.
expected_tradeoffs: small decomposition vs locality/deep cohesive behavior
verification_expectations: Confirm parser behavior remains covered by tests.
Inspect whether any candidate extraction has an independent contract or reason to change.
Compare the readable flow before and after extraction rather than relying on function length.
revisit_when: A parsing subproblem develops an independent reason to change.
A helper becomes reusable behind a stable meaningful contract.
The current function begins mixing unrelated abstraction levels or policies.
notes: Grounded in Clean Code 2e Chapters 7 and 10 plus the appendix Martin/Ousterhout method-length debate.
